newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Stals says liquidity squeeze not ended.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Stals says liquidity squeeze not ended.

text.p: It was premature to suggest that the recent decline in the money market shortage signalled an end to the liquidity squeeze, Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said on Tuesday.
On Monday, the shortage fell to 6.743 billion rand -- its lowest level since September 25 last year -- prompting commercial banks to reduce their deposit rates.
Call rates have also fallen below the 16.00 percent level as result of the improved liquidity to trade at between 15.50 and 15.75 percent.

Stals told Reuters that the shortage had fallen since the end of March on the back of increased reserves, which stood at 13.1 billion rand at the end of March, and a decrease in notes and coins in circulation.

"The money market shortage declined since the end of March (Easter weekend) because of a relatively large return-flow of notes and coins in circulation, and some increase in the foreign reserves," Stals said.
But he added: "It is premature to say that this signals the end of the liquidity squeeze."
Some money market traders believe that the improved liquidity in the market gives scope for both call and deposit rates to fall further.
They have also speculated that the imminent inflow of the $1 billion proceeds from the sale of a strategic equity stake in telecommunications utility Telkom could further reduce the shortage.
While he did not provide details on the Telkom transaction, Stals said the money market effects of the transaction would be managed "with normal monetary policy instruments at our disposal..."

These could include open market operations, switches in Corporation for Public Deposits (CPD) deposits and investments, short-term repurchase transactions, foreign currency/rand swaps, and switches of Government deposits between the Exchequer Account and Tax and Loan Accounts with banking institutions.
Asked if he agreed with the growing consensus among economists that an interest rate cut was only likely later this year, Stals said:

"The level of interest rates will depend on market movements, such as changes in overall liquidity, the rate of increase in bank credit extension and the money supply, the overall balance of payments situation, and trends in inflation and inflation expectations."
March consumer inflation, which will be released at 0900 GMT on Wednesday, is expected to show a 9.7 percent year-on-year or 0.7 percent month-on-month increase.
Economists believe that the March data should represent the peak in inflation before it heads lower during the rest of this year.
Latest money supply and credit extension data will be released at 1500 GMT on Friday.

Money supply growth is expected to show a 15.04 rise from February's preliminary 15.82 percent increase and private sector credit extension growth is seen rising 16.50 percent from a previous 17.34 percent.

On the balance of payments, Stals said that it was expected that a smaller current account deficit this year compared with the 8.5 billion rand deficit in 1996 would easily be covered by a net capital inflow.
Bank rate, the official lending rate, currently stands at 17 percent. It was last hiked by one percentage point on November 21 last year.
